entries.00cd4d064f4fdaf9c0ae9dc1a4051ea4cdf508f7: <div sID="gen15340" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="Song.7" sID="Song.7"/> <div eID="gen15340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15341" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15342" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, I. Christ, the royal bridegroom, goes on to describe the beauties of his spouse, the church, in many instances, and to express his love to her and the delight he has in her conversation, <reference osisRef="Song.7.1-Song.7.9">ver. 1-9</reference>. II. The spouse, the church, expresses her great delight in him, and the desire that she had of communion and fellowship with him, <reference osisRef="Song.7.10-Song.7.13">ver. 10-13</reference>. Such mutual esteem and endearment are there between Christ and believers. And what is heaven but an everlasting interchanging of loves between the holy God and holy souls!
entries.d923659fa7bc507cbe4214f7e9c8136c6e306066: <div eID="gen15342" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15341" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Beauty of the Church; The Complacency of Christ in His Church.</title> <div sID="gen15343" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> How beautiful are thy feet with shoes, O prince's daughter! the joints of thy thighs <hi type="italic">are</hi> like jewels, the work of the hands of a cunning workman. <hi type="super">2</hi> Thy navel <hi type="italic">is like</hi> a round goblet, <hi type="italic">which</hi> wanteth not liquor: thy belly <hi type="italic">is like</hi> a heap of wheat set about with lilies. <hi type="super">3</hi> Thy two breasts <hi type="italic">are</hi> like two young roes <hi type="italic">that are</hi> twins. <hi type="super">4</hi> Thy neck <hi type="italic">is</hi> as a tower of ivory; thine eyes <hi type="italic">like</hi> the fishpools in Heshbon, by the gate of Bath-rabbim: thy nose <hi type="italic">is</hi> as the tower of Lebanon which looketh toward Damascus. <hi type="super">5</hi> Thine head upon thee <hi type="italic">is</hi> like Carmel, and the hair of thine head like purple; the king <hi type="italic">is</hi> held in the galleries. <hi type="super">6</hi> How fair and how pleasant art thou, O love, for delights! <hi type="super">7</hi> This thy stature is like to a palm tree, and thy breasts to clusters <hi type="italic">of grapes.</hi> <hi type="super">8</hi> I said, I will go up to the palm tree, I will take hold of the boughs thereof: now also thy breasts shall be as clusters of the vine, and the smell of thy nose like apples; <hi type="super">9</hi> And the roof of thy mouth like the best wine for my beloved, that goeth <hi type="italic">down</hi> sweetly, causing the lips of those that are asleep to speak. <div eID="gen15343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15344" type="x-p"/> The title which Jesus Christ here gives to the church is new: <hi type="italic">O prince's daughter!</hi> agreeing with <reference osisRef="Ps.45.13">Ps. xlv. 13</reference>, where she is called <hi type="italic">the king's daughter.</hi> She is so in respect of her new birth, born from above, begotten of God, and his workmanship, bearing the image of the King of kings, and guided by his Spirit. She is so by marriage; Christ, by betrothing her to himself, though he found her mean and despicable, has made her a <hi type="italic">prince's daughter.</hi> She has a princely disposition, something in her truly noble and generous; she is daughter and heir to the prince of the kings of the earth. <hi type="italic">If children, then heirs.</hi> Now here we have, <div eID="gen15344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15345" type="x-p"/> I. A copious description of the beauty of the spouse, which, some think, is given by the virgins her companions, and that those were they who called upon her to return; it seems rather to be given by Christ himself, and to be designed to express his love to her and delight in her, as before, <reference osisRef="Song.4.1">ch. iv. 1</reference>, &c., and <reference osisRef="Song.6.5-Song.6.6">ch. vi. 5, 6</reference>. The similitudes are here different from what they were before, to show that the beauty of holiness is such as nothing in nature can reach; you may still say more of it, and yet still come short of it. That commendation of the spouse, <reference osisRef="Song.4.1-Song.4.16">ch. iv.</reference>, was immediately upon the espousals (<reference osisRef="Song.3.11">ch. iii. 11</reference>), this upon her return from a by-path (<reference osisRef="Song.6.13">ch. vi. 13</reference>); yet this exceeds that, to show the constancy of Christ's love to his people; <hi type="italic">he loves them to the end,</hi> since he made them <hi type="italic">precious in his sight and honourable.</hi> The spouse had described the beauty of her beloved in ten particulars (<reference osisRef="Song.5.11">ch. v. 11</reference>, &c.); and now he describes her in as many, for he will not be behindhand with her in respects and endearments. Those that honour Christ he will certainly honour, and make honourable. As the prophet, in describing the corruptions of degenerate Israel, reckons <hi type="italic">from the sole of the foot even unto the head</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.6">Isa. i. 6</reference>), so here the beauties of the church are reckoned from foot to head, that, as the apostle speaks, when he is comparing the church, as here, to the natural body (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.23">1 Cor. xii. 23</reference>), <hi type="italic">more abundant honour</hi> might be bestowed on those parts <hi type="italic">of the body which we think to be less honourable,</hi> and which therefore <hi type="italic">lacked honour,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.7.24">v. 24</reference>. 1. Her <hi type="italic">feet</hi> are here praised; the feet of Christ's ministers are beautiful in the eyes of the church (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.7">Isa. lii. 7</reference>), and her feet are here said to be beautiful in the eyes of Christ. <hi type="italic">How beautiful are thy feet with shoes!</hi> When believers, being made free from the captivity of sin (<reference osisRef="Acts.12.8">Acts xii. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">stand fast in the liberty with which they are made free,</hi> preserve the tokens of their enfranchisement, have <hi type="italic">their feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace,</hi> and walk steadily according to the rule of the gospel, then their <hi type="italic">feet are beautiful with shoes;</hi> they tread firmly, being well armed against the troubles they meet with in their way. When we rest not in good affections, but they are accompanied with sincere endeavors and resolutions, then our feet are beautified <hi type="italic">with shoes.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.10">Ezek. xvi. 10</reference>. 2. <hi type="italic">The joint of the thighs are</hi> here said to be <hi type="italic">like jewels,</hi> and those curiously wrought by <hi type="italic">a cunning workman.</hi> This is explained by <reference osisRef="Eph.4.16">Eph. iv. 16</reference> and <reference osisRef="Col.2.19">Col. ii. 19</reference>, where the mystical body of Christ is said to be held together by <hi type="italic">joints and bands,</hi> as the hips and knees (both which are <hi type="italic">the joints of the thighs</hi>) serve the natural body in its strength and motion. The church is <hi type="italic">then</hi> comely in Christ's eyes when those joints are kept firm by holy love and unity, and the communion of saints. When believers act in religion from good principles, and are steady and regular in their whole conversation, and turn themselves easily to every duty in its time and place, then <hi type="italic">the joints are like jewels.</hi> 3. The <hi type="italic">navel</hi> is here compared to a round cup or <hi type="italic">goblet,</hi> that <hi type="italic">wants not</hi> any of the agreeable <hi type="italic">liquor</hi> that one would wish to find in it, such as David's cup that ran over (<reference osisRef="Ps.23.5">Ps. xxiii. 5</reference>), well shaped, and not as that miserable infant whose navel was not cut, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.4">Ezek. xvi. 4</reference>. The fear of the Lord is said to be <hi type="italic">health to the navel.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Prov.3.8">Prov. iii. 8</reference>. When the soul wants not that fear then the <hi type="italic">navel wants not liquor.</hi> 4. The <hi type="italic">belly is like a heap of wheat</hi> in the store-chamber, which perhaps was sometimes, to make show, adorned with flowers. The <hi type="italic">wheat</hi> is useful, the <hi type="italic">lilies</hi> are beautiful; there is every thing in the church which may be to the members of that body either for use or for ornament. All the body is nourished from the <hi type="italic">belly;</hi> it denotes the spiritual prosperity of a believer and the healthful constitution of the soul all in good plight. 5. The <hi type="italic">breasts are like two young roes that are twins,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.7.3">v. 3</reference>. By the breasts of the church's consolations those are nourished who are born from its belly (<reference osisRef="Isa.46.3">Isa. xlvi. 3</reference>), and by the navel received nourishment in the womb. This comparison we had before, <reference osisRef="Song.4.5">ch. iv. 5</reference>. 6. The <hi type="italic">neck,</hi> which before was compared to <hi type="italic">the tower of David</hi> (<reference osisRef="Song.4.4">ch. iv. 4</reference>), is here compared to <hi type="italic">a tower of ivory,</hi> so white, so precious; such is the faith of the saints, by which they are joined to Christ their head. The name of the Lord, improved by faith, is to the saints as a strong and impregnable tower. 7. The <hi type="italic">eyes</hi> are compared to <hi type="italic">the fish-pools in Heshbon,</hi> or the artificial fish-ponds, <hi type="italic">by a gate,</hi> either of Jerusalem or Heshbon, which is called <hi type="italic">Bath-rabbim,</hi> the daughter of a multitude, because a great thoroughfare. The understanding, the intentions of a believer, are clean and clear as these ponds. The eyes, weeping for sin, are as fountains (<reference osisRef="Jer.9.1">Jer. ix. 1</reference>), and comely with Christ. 8. The <hi type="italic">nose</hi> is like <hi type="italic">the tower of Lebanon,</hi> the forehead or face set <hi type="italic">like a flint</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.7">Isa. l. 7</reference>), undaunted as that tower was impregnable. So it denotes the magnanimity and holy bravery of the church, or (as others) a spiritual sagacity to discern things that differ, as animals strangely distinguish by the smell. This tower <hi type="italic">looks towards Damascus,</hi> the head city of Syria, denoting the boldness of the church in facing its enemies and not fearing them. 9. The <hi type="italic">head like Carmel,</hi> a very high hill near the sea, <reference osisRef="Song.7.5">v. 5</reference>. The head of a believer is <hi type="italic">lifted up above his enemies</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.27.6">Ps. xxvii. 6</reference>), above the storms of the lower region, as the top of Carmel was, pointing heaven-ward. The more we get above this world, and the nearer to heaven, and the more secure and serene we become by that means, the more amiable we are in the eyes of the Lord Jesus. 10. <hi type="italic">The hair of the head</hi> is said to be <hi type="italic">like purple.</hi> This denotes the universal amiableness of a believer in the eyes of Christ, even to <hi type="italic">the hair,</hi> or (as some understand it) the pins with which <hi type="italic">the hair</hi> is dressed. Some by <hi type="italic">the head and the hair</hi> understand the governors of the church, who, if they be careful to do their duty, add much to her comeliness. <hi type="italic">The head like crimson</hi> (so some read it) <hi type="italic">and the hair like purple,</hi> the two colours worn by great men. <div eID="gen15345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15346" type="x-p"/> II. The complacency which Christ takes in his church thus beautified and adorned. She is lovely indeed if she be so in his eyes; as he puts the comeliness upon her, so it is his love that makes this comeliness truly valuable, for he is an unexceptionable judge. 1. He delighted to look upon his church, and to converse with it, rejoicing in that habitable part of his earth: <hi type="italic">The king is held in the galleries,</hi> and cannot leave them. This is explained by <reference osisRef="Ps.132.13-Ps.132.14">Ps. cxxxii. 13, 14</reference>, <hi type="italic">The Lord has chosen Zion,</hi> saying, <hi type="italic">This is my rest for ever;</hi> <hi type="italic">here will I dwell;</hi> and <reference osisRef="Ps.147.11">Ps. cxlvii. 11</reference>, <hi type="italic">The Lord takes pleasure in those that fear him.</hi> And, if Christ has such delight <hi type="italic">in the galleries</hi> of communion with his people, much more reason have they to delight in them, and to reckon <hi type="italic">a day there better than a thousand.</hi> 2. He was even struck with admiration at the beauty of his church (<reference osisRef="Song.7.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">How fair and how pleasant art thou, O love!</hi> <hi type="italic">How art thou made fair!</hi> (so the word is), "not born so, but made so with the comeliness which I have put upon thee." Holiness is a beauty beyond expression; the Lord Jesus is wonderfully pleased with it; the outward aspect of it is fair; the inward disposition of it is pleasant and highly agreeable, and the complacency he has in it is inexpressible. <hi type="italic">O my dearest for delights!</hi> so some read. 3. He determined to keep up communion with his church. (1.) To <hi type="italic">take hold of her</hi> as of <hi type="italic">the boughs of a palm-tree.</hi> He compares her <hi type="italic">stature to a palm-tree</hi> (<reference osisRef="Song.7.7">v. 7</reference>), so straight, so strong, does she appear, when she is looked upon in her full proportion. The <hi type="italic">palm-tree</hi> is observed to flourish most when it is loaded; so the church, the more it has been afflicted, the more it has multiplied; and the branches of it are emblems of victory. Christ says, "<hi type="italic">I will go up to the palm-tree,</hi> to entertain myself with the shadow of it (<reference osisRef="Song.7.8">v. 8</reference>) and <hi type="italic">I will take hold of its boughs</hi> and observe the beauty of them." What Christ has said he will do, in favour to his people; we may be sure he will do it, for his kind purposes are never suffered to fall to the ground; and if he <hi type="italic">take hold of the boughs</hi> of his church, take early hold of her branches, when they are young and tender, he will keep his hold and not let them go. (2.) To refresh himself with her fruits. He compares her <hi type="italic">breasts</hi> (her pious affections towards him) <hi type="italic">to clusters of grapes,</hi> a most pleasant fruit (<reference osisRef="Song.7.7">v. 7</reference>), and he repeats it (<reference osisRef="Song.7.8">v. 8</reference>): They <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> (that is, they shall be to me) <hi type="italic">as clusters of the vine,</hi> which <hi type="italic">make glad the heart.</hi> "Now that I come <hi type="italic">up to the palm-tree</hi> thy graces shall be exerted and excited." Christ's presence with his people kindles the holy heavenly fire in their souls, and then their <hi type="italic">breasts shall be as clusters of the vine,</hi> a cordial to themselves and acceptable to him. And since God, at first, <hi type="italic">breathed into man's nostrils the breath of life,</hi> and breathes the breath of the new life still, <hi type="italic">the smell of</hi> their nostrils is <hi type="italic">like the smell of apples,</hi> or oranges, which is pleasing and reviving. <hi type="italic">The Lord smelt a sweet savour</hi> from Noah's sacrifice, <reference osisRef="Gen.8.21">Gen. viii. 21</reference>. And, <hi type="italic">lastly, the roof of her mouth is like the best wine</hi> (<reference osisRef="Song.7.9">v. 9</reference>); her spiritual taste and relish, or the words she speaks of God and man, which come not from the teeth outward, but from <hi type="italic">the roof of the mouth,</hi> these are pleasing to God. <hi type="italic">The prayer of the upright is his delight.</hi> And, when <hi type="italic">those that fear the Lord speak one to another</hi> as becomes them, <hi type="italic">the Lord hearkens, and hears</hi> with pleasure, <reference osisRef="Mal.3.16">Mal. iii. 16</reference>. It is like that wine which is, [1.] Very palatable and grateful to the taste. It <hi type="italic">goes down sweetly;</hi> it <hi type="italic">goes straightly</hi> (so the margin reads it); it <hi type="italic">moves itself aright,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.23.31">Prov. xxiii. 31</reference>. The pleasures of sense seem right to the carnal appetite, and go down smoothly, but they are often wrong, and, compared with the pleasure of communion with God, they are harsh and rough. Nothing <hi type="italic">goes down so sweetly</hi> with a gracious soul as the wine of God's consolations. [2.] It is a great cordial. The presence of Christ by his Spirit with him people shall be reviving and refreshing to them, as that strong wine which makes <hi type="italic">the lips</hi> even <hi type="italic">of those that are asleep</hi> (that are ready to faint away in a deliquium), <hi type="italic">to speak.</hi> Unconverted sinners are asleep; saints are often drowsy, and listless, and half asleep; but the word and Spirit of Christ will put life and vigour into the soul, and <hi type="italic">out of the abundance of the heart</hi> that is thus filled<hi type="italic">the mouth</hi> will <hi type="italic">speak.</hi> When the apostles were filled with the Spirit they spoke <hi type="italic">with tongues the wonderful works of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.10">Acts ii. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.12">12</reference>); and those who in opposition to being <hi type="italic">drunk with wine, wherein is excess,</hi> are <hi type="italic">filled with the Spirit, speak to themselves in psalms and hymns,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.5.18-Eph.5.19">Eph. v. 18, 19</reference>. When Christ is thus commending the sweetness of his spouse's love, excited by the manifestation of his, she seems to put in that word, <hi type="italic">for my beloved,</hi> as in a parenthesis. "Is there any thing in me that is pleasant or valuable? As it is from, so it is for my beloved." <hi type="italic">Then</hi> he delights in our good affections and services, when they are all for him and devoted to his glory.
entries.681d3fcb7d004c8bd57cb52255f4516ac04cc7f2: <div eID="gen15346" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Desiring Communion with Christ; The Love of the Church to Christ.</title> <div sID="gen15347" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> I <hi type="italic">am</hi> my beloved's, and his desire <hi type="italic">is</hi> toward me. <hi type="super">11</hi> Come, my beloved, let us go forth into the field; let us lodge in the villages. <hi type="super">12</hi> Let us get up early to the vineyards; let us see if the vine flourish, <hi type="italic">whether</hi> the tender grape appear, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the pomegranates bud forth: there will I give thee my loves. <hi type="super">13</hi> The mandrakes give a smell, and at our gates <hi type="italic">are</hi> all manner of pleasant <hi type="italic">fruits,</hi> new and old, <hi type="italic">which</hi> I have laid up for thee, O my beloved. <div eID="gen15347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15348" type="x-p"/> These are the words of the spouse, the church, the believing soul, in answer to the kind expressions of Christ's love in the foregoing verses. <div eID="gen15348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15349" type="x-p"/> I. She here triumphs in her relation to Christ and her interest in him, and in his name will she boast all the day long. With what a transport of joy and holy exultation does she say (<reference osisRef="Song.7.10">v. 10</reference>), "<hi type="italic">I am my beloved's,</hi> not my own, but entirely devoted to him and owned by him." If we can truly say that Christ is our <hi type="italic">best beloved,</hi> we may be confident that we are his and he <hi type="italic">will save us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.119.94">Ps. cxix. 94</reference>. The gracious discoveries of Christ's love to us should engage us greatly to rejoice in the hold he has of us, his sovereignty over us and property in us, which is no less a spring of comfort than a bond of duty. Intimacy of communion with Christ should help clear up our interest in him. Glorying in this, that she is his, to serve him, and reckoning that her honour, she comforts herself with this, that his <hi type="italic">desire is towards her,</hi> that is, he is her husband; it is a periphrasis of the conjugal relation, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.16">Gen. iii. 16</reference>. Christ's desire was strongly towards his chosen remnant, when he came from heaven to earth to seek and save them; and when, in pursuance of his undertaking, he was even straitened till the baptism of blood he was to pass through for them <hi type="italic">was accomplished,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.12.50">Luke xii. 50</reference>. He desired <hi type="italic">Zion for a habitation;</hi> this is a comfort to believers that, whosoever slights them, Christ has a desire towards them, such a desire as will again bring him from heaven to earth to receive them to himself; for he longs to have them all with him, <reference osisRef="John.17.24">John xvii. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.14.3">xiv. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen15349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15350" type="x-p"/> II. She humbly and earnestly desires communion with him (<reference osisRef="Song.7.11-Song.7.12">v. 11, 12</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Come, my beloved,</hi> let us take a walk together, that I may receive counsel, instruction, and comfort from thee, and may make known my wants and grievances to thee, with freedom, and without interruption." Thus Christ can walk with the two disciples that were going to the village called <hi type="italic">Emmaus,</hi> and talked with them, till he made their <hi type="italic">hearts burn within them.</hi> Observe here, 1. Having received fresh tokens of his love, and full assurances of her interest in him, she presses forward towards further acquaintance with him; as blessed Paul, who desired yet more and more of <hi type="italic">the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.3.8">Phil. iii. 8</reference>. Christ has made it to appear how much his desire is towards us, and we are very ungrateful if ours be not towards him. Note, Communion with Christ is that which all that are sanctified earnestly breathe after; and the clearer discoveries he makes to them of his love the more earnestly do they desire it. Sensual pleasures pall the carnal appetite, and soon give it surfeit, but spiritual delights whet the desires, the language of which is, <hi type="italic">Nothing more than God,</hi> but still <hi type="italic">more and more of him.</hi> Christ had said, <hi type="italic">I will go up to the palm-tree.</hi> Come, saith she, <hi type="italic">Let us go.</hi> The promises Christ has made us of communion with him are not to supersede, but quicken and encourage, our prayers for that communion. 2. She desires to go forth into the fields and villages to have this communion with him. Those that would converse with Christ must go forth from the world and the amusements of it, must avoid every thing that would divert the mind and be a hindrance to it when it should be wholly taken up with Christ; we must contrive how to <hi type="italic">attend upon the Lord without distraction</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.35">1 Cor. vii. 35</reference>), for therefore the spouse here covets to get out of the noise of the town. <hi type="italic">Let us go forth to him without the camp,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.14.13">Heb. xiv. 13</reference>. Solitude and retirement befriend communion with God; therefore <hi type="italic">Isaac went out into the field to meditate</hi> and pray. <hi type="italic">Enter into thy closet, and shut thy door.</hi> A believer is never less alone than when alone with Christ, where no eye sees. 3. Having business to go abroad, to look after their grounds, she desires the company of her beloved. Note, Wherever we are, we may keep up our communion with God, if it be not our own fault, for he is always at our right hand, his eye always upon us, and both his word and his ear always nigh us. By going about our worldly affairs with heavenly holy hearts, mixing pious thoughts with common actions, and having our eyes ever towards the Lord, we may take Christ along with us whithersoever we go. Nor should we go any whither where we cannot in faith ask him to go along with us. 4. She is willing to rise betimes, to go along with her beloved: <hi type="italic">Let us get up early to the vineyards.</hi> It intimates her care to improve opportunities of conversing with her beloved; when the time appointed has come, we must lose no time, but, as the woman (<reference osisRef="Mark.16.2">Mark xvi. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">go very early,</hi> though it be to a <hi type="italic">sepulchre,</hi> if we be in hopes to meet him there. Those that will go abroad with Christ must begin betimes with him, early in the morning of their days, must begin every day with him, seek him early, seek him diligently. 5. She will be content to take up her lodging in the villages, the huts or cottages which the country people built for their shelter when they attended their business in the fields; there, in these mean and cold dwellings, she will gladly reside, if she may but have her beloved with her. His presence will make them fine and pleasant, and convert them into palaces. A gracious soul can reconcile itself to the poorest accommodations, if it may have communion with God in them. 6. The most pleasant delightful fields, even in the spring-time, when the country is most pleasant, will not satisfy her, unless she have her beloved with her. No delights on earth can make a believer easy, unless he enjoy God in all. <div eID="gen15350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15351" type="x-p"/> III. She desires to be better acquainted with the state of her own soul and the present posture of its affairs (<reference osisRef="Song.7.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let us see if the vine flourish.</hi> Our own souls are our vineyards; they are, or should be, planted with vines and pomegranates, choice and useful trees. We are made keepers of these vineyards, and therefore are concerned often to look into them, to examine the state of our own souls, to seek whether the <hi type="italic">vine flourishes,</hi> whether our graces be in act and exercise, whether we be fruitful in the fruits of righteousness, and whether our fruit abound. And especially let us enquire whether <hi type="italic">the tender grape appear</hi> and whether <hi type="italic">the pomegranates bud forth,</hi> what good motions and dispositions there are in us that are yet but young and tender, that they may be protected and cherished with a particular care, and may not be nipped, or blasted, or rubbed off, but cultivated, that they may bring forth fruit unto perfection. In this enquiry into our own spiritual state, it will be good to take Christ along with us, because his presence will make the <hi type="italic">vine flourish</hi> and the <hi type="italic">tender grape appear,</hi> as the returning sun revives the gardens, and because to him we are concerned to approve ourselves. If he sees the <hi type="italic">vine flourish,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">tender grape appear</hi>—if we can appeal to him, <hi type="italic">Thou knowest all things, thou knowest that I love thee,</hi>—if his Spirit witness with our spirit that our souls prosper, it is enough. And, if we would be acquainted with ourselves, we must beg of him to search and try us, to help us in the search, and discover us to ourselves. <div eID="gen15351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15352" type="x-p"/> IV. She promises to her beloved the best entertainment she can give him at her country seat; for he will come in to us, and sup with us, <reference osisRef="Rev.3.20">Rev. iii. 20</reference>. 1. She promises him her best affections; and, whatever else she had for him, it would utterly be contemned if her heart were not entire for him: "<hi type="italic">There</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">will I give thee my love;</hi> I will repeat the professions of it, honour thee with the tokens of it; and the out-goings of my soul towards thee in adorations and desires shall be quickened and enlarged, and my heart offered up to thee in a holy fire." 2. She promises him her best provision, <reference osisRef="Song.7.13">v. 13</reference>. "There we shall find pleasant odours, for <hi type="italic">the mandrakes give a smell;</hi>" the <hi type="italic">love-flowers</hi> or <hi type="italic">lovely ones</hi> (so the word signifies), or the <hi type="italic">love-fruits;</hi> it was something that was in all respects very grateful, so valuable that Rachel and Leah had like to have fallen out above it, <reference osisRef="Gen.30.14">Gen. xxx. 14</reference>. "We shall also find that which is good for food, as well as pleasant to the eye, all the rarities that the country affords: <hi type="italic">At our gates are all manner of pleasant fruits.</hi>" Note, (1.) The fruits and exercises of grace are pleasant to the Lord Jesus. (2.) These must be carefully laid up for him, devoted to his service and honour, must be always ready to us when we have occasion for them, as that which is laid up at our gates, that, by our bringing forth much fruit, he may be glorified, <reference osisRef="John.15.18">John xv. 18</reference>. (3.) There is a great variety of these pleasant fruits, with which our souls should be well stocked; we must have all sorts of them, grace for all occasions, <hi type="italic">new and old,</hi> as the good householder has in his treasury, not only the products of this year, but remainders of the last, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.52">Matt. xiii. 52</reference>. We must not only have that ready to us, for the service of Christ, which we have heard, and learned, and experienced lately, but must retain that which we have formerly gathered; nor must we content ourselves only with what we have laid up in store in the days of old, but, as long as we live, must be still adding something new to it, that our stock may increase, and we may be <hi type="italic">thoroughly furnished for every good work.</hi> (4.) Those that truly love Christ will think all they have, even their most <hi type="italic">pleasant fruits,</hi> and what they have treasured up most carefully, too little to be bestowed upon him, and he is welcome to it all; if it were more and better, it should be at his service. It is all from him, and therefore it is fit it should be all for him.  <chapter eID="Song.7"/> <div eID="gen15352" type="x-p"/>

entries.e6d24ddc9d06dc5b244e6bab862e87a1c3796fca: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8281"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 7</title> <div sID="gen13112" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Song.7.1-Song.7.13">So 7:1-13</reference>.<div eID="gen13112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13113" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8281"/><hi type="bold">1. thy feet--</hi>rather, "thy goings" (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.5">Psa 17:5</reference>). Evident allusion to <reference osisRef="Isa.52.7">Is 52:7</reference>: "How beautiful ... are the feet of him ... that publisheth peace" (Shulamite, <reference osisRef="Song.6.13">So 6:13</reference>).<div eID="gen13113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13114" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shoes--</hi>Sandals are richly jewelled in the East (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.22">Lu 15:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.6.15">Ep 6:15</reference>). She is evidently "on the mountains," whither she was wafted (<reference osisRef="Song.6.12">So 6:12</reference>), above the daughters of Jerusalem, who therefore portray her feet first.<div eID="gen13114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13115" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">daughter--</hi>of God the Father, with whom Jesus Christ is one (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.9">Mt 5:9</reference>), "children of (the) God" (of peace), equivalent to Shulamite (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.10-Ps.45.15">Psa 45:10-15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.18">2Co 6:18</reference>), as well as bride of Jesus Christ.<div eID="gen13115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13116" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prince's--</hi>therefore princely herself, freely giving the word of life to others, not sparing her "feet," as in <reference osisRef="Song.5.3">So 5:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.12.11">Ex 12:11</reference>. To act on the offensive is defensive to ourselves.<div eID="gen13116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13117" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">joints--</hi>rather, "the rounding"; the full graceful curve of the hips in the female figure; like the rounding of a necklace (as the Hebrew for "jewels" means). Compare with the English Version, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.13-Eph.4.16">Ep 4:13-16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.19">Col 2:19</reference>. Or, applying it to the girdle binding together the robes round the hips (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.14">Ep 6:14</reference>).<div eID="gen13117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13118" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cunning workman--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.139.14-Ps.139.16">Psa 139:14-16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.10">Ep 2:10</reference>, 22; 5:29, 30, 32). <div eID="gen13118" type="x-p"/>
entries.c9353e5d419bf7a87ca29bd1c44cb95a48fa75d2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8282"/><div sID="gen13119" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8282"/><hi type="bold">2. navel--</hi>rather, "girdle-clasp," called from the part of the person underneath. The "shoes" (<reference osisRef="Song.7.1">So 7:1</reference>) prove that dress is throughout presupposed on all parts where it is usually worn. She is "a bride adorned for her husband"; the "uncomely parts," being most adorned (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.23">1Co 12:23</reference>). The girdle-clasp was adorned with red rubies resembling the "round goblet" (crater or mixer) of spice-mixed wine (not "liquor," <reference osisRef="Song.8.2">So 8:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.22">Is 5:22</reference>). The wine of the "New Testament in His blood" (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.20">Lu 22:20</reference>). The spiritual exhilaration by it was mistaken for that caused by new wine (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.13-Acts.2.17">Ac 2:13-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.18">Ep 5:18</reference>).<div eID="gen13119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13120" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">belly--</hi>that is, the vesture on it. As in <reference osisRef="Ps.45.13">Psa 45:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.14">14</reference>, gold and needlework compose the bride's attire, so golden-colored "wheat" and white "lilies" here. The ripe grain, in token of harvest joy, used to be decorated with lilies; so the accumulated spiritual food (<reference osisRef="John.6.35">Joh 6:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.24">12:24</reference>), free from chaff, not fenced with thorns, but made attractive by lilies ("believers," <reference osisRef="Song.2.2">So 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.46">Ac 2:46</reference>, 47; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.13">5:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.14">14</reference>, in common partaking of it). Associated with the exhilarating wine cup (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.17">Zec 9:17</reference>), as here. <div eID="gen13120" type="x-p"/>
entries.8774e4131fc2b5e0212cc1d00c79b6adcc1f9f14: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8283"/><div sID="gen13121" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8283"/>3. The daughters of Jerusalem describe her in the same terms as Jesus Christ in <reference osisRef="Song.4.5">So 4:5</reference>. The testimonies of heaven and earth coincide.<div eID="gen13121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13122" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">twins--</hi>faith and love. <div eID="gen13122" type="x-p"/>
entries.4154dd4462f5904b2a5516e63790c15e944dda8e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8284"/><div sID="gen13123" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8284"/><hi type="bold">4. tower of ivory--</hi>In <reference osisRef="Song.4.4">So 4:4</reference>, Jesus Christ saith, "a tower of David builded for an armory." Strength and conquest are the main thought in His description; here, beauty and polished whiteness; contrast <reference osisRef="Song.1.5">So 1:5</reference>.<div eID="gen13123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13124" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fishpools--</hi>seen by Burckhardt, clear (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.1">Re 22:1</reference>), deep, quiet, and full (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.10">1Co 2:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.15">15</reference>).<div eID="gen13124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13125" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Heshbon--</hi>east of Jordan, residence of the Amorite king, Sihon (<reference osisRef="Num.21.25">Nu 21:25</reference>, &c.), afterwards held by Gad.<div eID="gen13125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13126" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Bath-rabbim--</hi>"daughter of a multitude"; a crowded thoroughfare. Her eyes (<reference osisRef="Song.4.1">So 4:1</reference>) are called by Jesus Christ, "doves' eyes," waiting on Him. But here, looked on by the daughters or Jerusalem, they are compared to a placid lake. She is calm even amidst the crowd (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.2">Pr 8:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.16.33">Joh 16:33</reference>).<div eID="gen13126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13127" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nose--</hi>or, face.<div eID="gen13127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13128" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tower of Lebanon--</hi>a border-fortress, watching the hostile Damascus. Towards Jesus Christ her face was full of holy shame (see on <reference osisRef="Song.4.1">So 4:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Song.4.3">So 4:3</reference>); towards spiritual foes, like a watchtower (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.1">Ha 2:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.13.37">Mr 13:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.4.13">Ac 4:13</reference>), elevated, so that she looks not up from earth to heaven, but down from heaven to earth. If we retain "nose," discernment of spiritual fragrance is meant. <div eID="gen13128" type="x-p"/>
entries.0b0b737e68171e1ea598befff8ce60ada0fe3114: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8285"/><div sID="gen13129" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8285"/><hi type="bold">5. upon thee--</hi>the headdress "upon" her.<div eID="gen13129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13130" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Carmel--</hi>signifying a well-cultivated field (<reference osisRef="Isa.35.2">Is 35:2</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Song.5.15">So 5:15</reference> He is compared to majestic Lebanon; she here, to fruitful Carmel. Her headdress, or crown (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.8">2Ti 4:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.4">1Pe 5:4</reference>). Also the souls won by her (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.19">1Th 2:19</reference>, 20), a token of her fruitfulness.<div eID="gen13130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13131" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">purple--</hi>royalty (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.6">Re 1:6</reference>). As applied to hair, it expresses the glossy splendor of black hair (literally, "pendulous hair") so much admired in the East (<reference osisRef="Song.4.1">So 4:1</reference>). While the King compares her hair to the flowering hair of goats (the token of her subjection), the daughters of Jerusalem compare it to royal purple.<div eID="gen13131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13132" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">galleries--</hi>(so <reference osisRef="Song.1.17">So 1:17</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.3">Re 21:3</reference>). But Maurer translates here, "flowing ringlets"; with these, as with "thongs" (so Lee, from the Arabic translates it) "the King is held" bound (<reference osisRef="Song.6.5">So 6:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.6.25">Pr 6:25</reference>). Her purple crowns of martyrdom especially captivated the King, appearing from His galleries (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.55">Ac 7:55</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.7.56">56</reference>). As Samson's strength was in his locks (<reference osisRef="Judg.16.17">Jud 16:17</reference>). Here first the daughters see the King themselves. <div eID="gen13132" type="x-p"/>
entries.58f645905152bac92c2d6d7ca51d3ed4e902798c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8286"/><div sID="gen13133" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8286"/>6. Nearer advance of the daughters to the Church (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.47">Ac 2:47</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.13">5:13</reference>, end). Love to her is the first token of love to Him (<reference osisRef="1John.5.1">1Jo 5:1</reference>, end).<div eID="gen13133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13134" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">delights--</hi>fascinating charms to them and to the King (<reference osisRef="Song.7.5">So 7:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.62.4">Is 62:4</reference>, Hephzi-bah). Hereafter, too (<reference osisRef="Zeph.3.17">Zep 3:17</reference>; Mal 3:12; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.9">Re 21:9</reference>). <div eID="gen13134" type="x-p"/>
entries.db5eb140785b15ee76342680a80bdaa8af4715b4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8287"/><div sID="gen13135" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8287"/><hi type="bold">7. palm tree--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.92.12">Psa 92:12</reference>). The sure sign of water near (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.27">Ex 15:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.7.38">Joh 7:38</reference>).<div eID="gen13135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13136" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">clusters--</hi>not of dates, as Moody Stuart thinks. The parallelism (<reference osisRef="Song.7.8">So 7:8</reference>), "clusters of the vine," shows it is here clusters of grapes. Vines were often trained (termed "wedded") on other trees. <div eID="gen13136" type="x-p"/>
entries.40c0dcf8c6aa6c445686196719777f6dd661c835: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8288"/><div sID="gen13137" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8288"/>8. The daughters are no longer content to admire, but resolve to lay hold of her fruits, high though these be. The palm stem is bare for a great height, and has its crown of fruit-laden boughs at the summit. It is the symbol of triumphant joy (<reference osisRef="John.12.13">Joh 12:13</reference>); so hereafter (<reference osisRef="Rev.7.9">Re 7:9</reference>).<div eID="gen13137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13138" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">breasts--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.66.11">Is 66:11</reference>).<div eID="gen13138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13139" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the vine--</hi>Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.7">Ho 14:7</reference>, end; <reference osisRef="John.15.1">Joh 15:1</reference>).<div eID="gen13139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13140" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nose--</hi>that is, breath; the Holy Ghost breathed into her nostrils by Him, whose "mouth is most sweet" (<reference osisRef="Song.5.16">So 5:16</reference>).<div eID="gen13140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13141" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">apples--</hi>citrons, off the tree to which He is likened (<reference osisRef="Song.2.3">So 2:3</reference>). <div eID="gen13141" type="x-p"/>
entries.cf4da6372fd0dfa0397e070cfbf3d3319e93dbd0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8289"/><div sID="gen13142" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8289"/><hi type="bold">9. roof of thy mouth--</hi>thy voice (<reference osisRef="Prov.15.23">Pr 15:23</reference>).<div eID="gen13142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13143" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">best wine--</hi>the new wine of the gospel kingdom (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.25">Mr 14:25</reference>), poured out at Pentecost (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.4">Ac 2:4</reference>, 13, 17).<div eID="gen13143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13144" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for my beloved--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Song.4.10">So 4:10</reference>). Here first the daughters call Him theirs, and become one with the bride. The steps successively are (<reference osisRef="Song.1.5">So 1:5</reference>) where they misjudge her (<reference osisRef="Song.3.11">So 3:11</reference>); <reference osisRef="Song.5.8">So 5:8</reference>, where the possibility of their finding Him, before she regained Him, is expressed; <reference osisRef="Song.5.9">So 5:9</reference> (<reference osisRef="Song.6.1">So 6:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Song.7.6">7:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Song.7.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.4.42">Joh 4:42</reference>).<div eID="gen13144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13145" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">causing ... asleep to speak--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.35.6">Is 35:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.5.19">Mr 5:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.5.20">20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.47">Ac 2:47</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.14">Ep 5:14</reference>). Jesus Christ's first miracle turned water into "good wine kept until now" (<reference osisRef="John.2.10">Joh 2:10</reference>); just as the Gospel revives those asleep and dying under the law (<reference osisRef="Prov.31.6">Pr 31:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.7.9">Ro 7:9</reference>, 10, 24, 25; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.1">8:1</reference>). <div eID="gen13145" type="x-p"/>
entries.9a9b77db755880442256be9be9fbc63bf9d3724c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8290"/><div sID="gen13146" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8290"/>10. Words of the daughters of Jerusalem and the bride, now united into one (<reference osisRef="Acts.4.32">Ac 4:32</reference>). They are mentioned again distinctly (<reference osisRef="Song.8.4">So 8:4</reference>), as fresh converts were being added from among enquirers, and these needed to be charged not to grieve the Spirit.<div eID="gen13146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13147" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his desire is toward me--</hi>strong assurance. He so desires us, as to give us sense of His desire toward us (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.17">Psa 139:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.18">18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.22.15">Lu 22:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.2.20">Ga 2:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.4.16">1Jo 4:16</reference>). <div eID="gen13147" type="x-p"/>
entries.f08a68195d481f6c1671d97e99ac09fb41d97de9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8291"/><div sID="gen13148" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8291"/><hi type="bold">11. field--</hi>the country. "The tender grape (Maurer translates, flowers) and vines" occurred before (<reference osisRef="Song.2.13">So 2:13</reference>). But here she prepares for Him all kinds of fruit old and new; also, she anticipates, in going forth to seek them, communion with Him in "loves." "Early" implies immediate earnestness. "The villages" imply distance from Jerusalem. At Stephen's death the disciples were scattered from it through Judea and Samaria, preaching the word (<reference osisRef="Acts.8.4-Acts.8.25">Ac 8:4-25</reference>). Jesus Christ was with them, confirming the word with miracles. They gathered the old fruits, of which Jesus Christ had sown the seed (<reference osisRef="John.4.39-John.4.42">Joh 4:39-42</reference>), as well as new fruits.<div eID="gen13148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13149" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lodge--</hi>forsaking home for Jesus Christ's sake (<reference osisRef="Matt.19.29">Mt 19:29</reference>). <div eID="gen13149" type="x-p"/>
entries.855434d3aa120c1480fe5f851d7b90e57c67e55f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8292"/><div sID="gen13150" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8292"/>12. (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.35">Mr 1:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.9.4">Joh 9:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.6.10">Ga 6:10</reference>). Assurance fosters diligence, not indolence. <div eID="gen13150" type="x-p"/>
entries.b0405517c90484821a4b03b62cb806e6a34ffcb4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8293"/><div sID="gen13151" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8293"/><hi type="bold">13. mandrakes--</hi>Hebrew, dudaim, from a root meaning "to love"; love apples, supposed to exhilarate the spirits and excite love. Only here and <reference osisRef="Gen.30.14-Gen.30.16">Ge 30:14-16</reference>. Atropa mandragora of Linnæus; its leaves like lettuce, but dark green, flowers purple, root forked, fruit of the size of an apple, ruddy and sweet-smelling, gathered in wheat harvest, that is, in May (Mariti, ii. 195).<div eID="gen13151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13152" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gates--</hi>the entrance to the kiosk or summer house. Love "lays up" the best of everything for the person beloved (<reference osisRef="1Cor.10.31">1Co 10:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.8">Php 3:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.11">1Pe 4:11</reference>), thereby really, though unconsciously, laying up for itself (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.18">1Ti 6:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.19">19</reference>). <chapter eID="Song.7"/>

entries.963d1f160f7dad6f2f1c7c2d577bfe3401f608b3: <div eID="gen26112" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen26113" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen26114" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26114" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26113" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen26115" type="x-p"/> A farther description of the bride, <reference osisRef="Sol.7.1-Sol.7.9">Sol 7:1-9</reference>. Her invitation to the bridegroom, <reference osisRef="Sol.7.10-Sol.7.13">Sol 7:10-13</reference>. <div eID="gen26115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26116" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen26116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26117" type="x-p"/> How beautiful are thy feet with shoes - "How graceful is thy walking." In the sixth chapter the bridegroom praises the Shulamite, as we might express it, from head to foot. Here he begins a new description, taking her from foot to head. <div eID="gen26117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26118" type="x-p"/> The shoes, sandals, or slippers of the Eastern ladies are most beautifully formed, and richly embroidered. The majestic walk of a beautiful woman in such shoes is peculiarly grand. And to show that such a walk is intended, he calls her a prince's daughter. <div eID="gen26118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26119" type="x-p"/> The joints of thy thighs - Must refer to the ornaments on the beautiful drawers, which are in general use among ladies of quality in most parts of the East.
entries.4bda99a21e5ca0ea8de364095697c45949e086af: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen26119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26120" type="x-p"/> Thy navel is like a round goblet - This may also refer to some ornamental dress about the loins. These suppositions are rendered very probable from hundreds of the best finished and highly decorated drawings of Asiatic ladies in my own collection, where every thing appears in the drawings, as in nature. <div eID="gen26120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26121" type="x-p"/> A heap of wheat set about with lilies - This is another instance of the same kind. The richly embroidered dresses in the above drawings may amply illustrate this also. Ainsworth supposes the metaphor is taken from a pregnant woman; the child in the womb being nourished by means of the umbilical cord or navel string, till it is brought into the world. After which it is fed by means of the mother's breasts, which are immediately mentioned. Possibly the whole may allude to the bride's pregnancy.
entries.eda56573c5f7e9fb73a6138b07993d38c5bec0ed: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen26121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26122" type="x-p"/> Thy two breasts - Where the hair and breasts are fine, they are the highest ornaments of the person of a female.
entries.7fed8a3da1174f60fd4c0c749a79911ecaa07eb6: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen26122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26123" type="x-p"/> Thy neck - as a tower of ivory - High, white, and ornamented with jewellery, as the tower of David was with bucklers. See on <reference osisRef="Sol.4.4">Sol 4:4</reference> (note). <div eID="gen26123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26124" type="x-p"/> The fish - pools in Heshbon - Clear, bright, and serene. These must have been very beautiful to have been introduced here in comparison. These two fountains appear to have been situated at the gate that led from Heshbon to Rabba, or Rabboth Ammon. There is a propriety in this metaphor, because fountains are considered to be the eyes of the earth. <div eID="gen26124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26125" type="x-p"/> Thy nose - as the tower of Lebanon - There was doubtless a propriety in this similitude also, which cannot now be discerned. If we are to understand the similitude as taken from the projecting form of the nose, even here I see nothing striking in the metaphor; for surely the tower of Lebanon did not project from the mountain as the human nose does from the face. It is better to acknowledge that there was undoubtedly some fit resemblances; but in what circumstance we know not. But some commentators are always extolling the correctness of the imagery in those very difficult places, where no soul sees the similitude but themselves.
entries.94770dd61a48530c4049857b261cd784bed42c48: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen26125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26126" type="x-p"/> Shine head - like Carmel - Rising majestically upon thy neck, and above thy shoulders, as Mount Carmel does in its district. Carmel was the name of the mountain where Elijah had his contest with the prophets of Baal. See <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.19">1Kgs 18:19</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen26126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26127" type="x-p"/> The hair of thine head like purple - Ornamented with ribbons and jewellery of this tint. <div eID="gen26127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26128" type="x-p"/> The king is held in the galleries - Or is detained in the antechamber. His heart is captivated by thy person and conduct. Some understand the ringlets of the bride's hair.
entries.97ee86bff4fea1020f3e0677959381fd1013c639: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen26128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26129" type="x-p"/> How fair and how pleasant - Thou art every way beautiful, and in every respect calculated to inspire pleasure and delight.
entries.ac4bda1dd980191441c077f50c8c2ffb362e615f: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen26129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26130" type="x-p"/> Like to a palm tree - Which is remarkably straight, taper, and elegant. <div eID="gen26130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26131" type="x-p"/> And thy breasts to clusters of grapes - Dates are the fruit of the palm tree; they grow in clusters; and it is these, not grapes, which are intended.
entries.d215eadd887b425e550d25bc92526977443a86f5: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen26131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26132" type="x-p"/> I will go up to the palm tree - I will take hold on the boughs of this tree, and climb up by them, in order to gather the clusters of dates at the top. The rubric here in the old MS. interprets this of the cross of Christ.
entries.3dd358db72fdc12a5af1e4799b3bd10658550795: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen26132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26133" type="x-p"/> The roof of thy mouth like the best wine - The voice or conversation of the spouse is most probably what is meant. <div eID="gen26133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26134" type="x-p"/> Causing the lips of those that are asleep to speak - As good wine has a tendency to cause the most backward to speak fluently when taken in moderation; so a sight of thee, and hearing the charms of thy conversation, is sufficient to excite the most taciturn to speak, and even to become eloquent in thy praises.
entries.9ef74a403431425368f00b95e0eda59a7a1deaf6: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen26134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26135" type="x-p"/> I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me - It is worthy of remark that the word which we translate his desire is the very same used <reference osisRef="Gen.3.16">Gen 3:16</reference> : Thy desire, thy ruling appetite, תשוקתך teshukathech, shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee. This was a part of the woman's curse. Now here it seems to be reversed; for the bride says, I am my beloved's, and his desire or ruling appetite and affection, תשוקתו teshukatho, is עלי ali, Upon Me. The old MS. translates this with considerable force: - "I to my leef, and to me the turnynge of him".
entries.2413836c5573ec869943445d5772b9e45a143839: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen26135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26136" type="x-p"/> Let us go forth into the field - It has been conjectured that the bridegroom arose early every morning, and left the bride's apartment, and withdrew to the country; often leaving her asleep, and commanding her companions not to disturb her till she should awake of herself. Here the bride wishes to accompany her spouse to the country, and spend a night at his country house.
entries.f4b416a3e8f6f44be209aa18c82f449b853ee3c0: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen26136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26137" type="x-p"/> Let us get up early to the vineyards - When in the country, we shall have the better opportunity to contemplate the progress of the spring vegetation; and there she promises to be peculiarly affectionate to him.
entries.c9a5de7987187c69a66f42d71212f58ce18790ca: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen26137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26138" type="x-p"/> The mandrakes give a smell - See the note on <reference osisRef="Gen.30.14">Gen 30:14</reference>, where the mandrake is particularly described; from which this passage will receive considerable light. The reader is requested to consult it. <div eID="gen26138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26139" type="x-p"/> All manner of pleasant fruits - Fruits new and old; flowers and herbs of every kind which the season could yield. The literal sense, allowing for the concealing metaphors, is, I believe, of a widely different nature from what is generally given. But this must be left to the reader's sagacity and prudence.  <chapter eID="Song.7"/> <div eID="gen26139" type="x-p"/>

entries.b7dbbc054796799697e50f430dc596e3ceeb5529: Sol 7:1 1 <hi type="italic">a</hi> How beautiful are thy steps in the shoes,      O prince’s daughter! <div eID="gen12666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12667" type="x-p"/> The noun נדיב, which signifies noble in disposition, and then noble by birth and rank (cf. the reverse relation of the meanings in <hi type="italic">generosus</hi>), is in the latter sense synon. and parallel to מלך and שׂר; Shulamith is here called a prince’s daughter because she was raised to the rank of which Hannah, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.8">1Sa 2:8</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.113.8">Psa 113:8</reference>, speaks, and to which she herself, 6:12 points. Her beauty, from the first associated with unaffected dignity, now appears in native princely grace and majesty. פּעם (from פּעם, <hi type="italic">pulsare</hi>, as <hi type="italic">in nunc pede libero pulsanda tellus</hi>) signifies step and foot, - in the latter sense the poet. Heb. and the vulgar Phoen. word for רגל; here the meanings <hi type="italic">pes</hi> and <hi type="italic">passus</hi> (Fr. <hi type="italic">pas</hi>, dance-step) flow into each other. The praise of the spectators now turns from the feet of the dancer to her thighs: 1 <hi type="italic">b</hi> The vibration of thy thighs like ornamental chains,      The work of an artist’s hands. <div eID="gen12667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12668" type="x-p"/> The double-sided thighs, viewed from the spine and the lower part of the back, are called מתנים; from the upper part of the legs upwards, and the breast downwards (the lumbar region), thus seen on the front and sidewise, חלצים or ירכים. Here the manifold twistings and windings of the upper part of the body by means of the thigh-joint are meant; such movements of a circular kind are called חמּוּקים, from חמק, Sol 5:6. חלאים is the plur. of חלי = (Arab.) ḥaly, as חבאים (gazelles) of צבי = zaby. The sing. חלי (or חליה = Arab. hulyah) signifies a female ornament, consisting of gold, silver, or precious stones, and that (according to the connection, <reference osisRef="Prov.25.2">Pro 25:2</reference>; Hos 2:15) for the neck or the breast as a whole; the plur. חל, occurring only here, is therefore chosen because the bendings of the loins, full of life and beauty, are compared to the free swingings to and fro of such an ornament, and thus to a connected ornament of chains; for חם are not the beauty-curves of the thighs at rest, - the connection here requires movement. In accordance with the united idea of חל, the appos. is not מעשׂי, but (according to the Palestin.) מעשׂה (lxx, Targ., Syr., Venet.). The artist is called אמּן (ommân) (the forms אמן and אמן are also found), Syr. avmon, Jewish-Aram. אוּמן; he has, as the master of stability, a name like ימין, the right hand: the hand, and especially the right hand, is the <hi type="italic">artifex</hi> among the members.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Ryssel’s <hi type="italic">Die Syn. d. Wahren u. Guten in d. Sem. Spr</hi>. (1873), p. 12.</note> <div eID="gen12668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12669" type="x-p"/> The eulogists pass from the loins to the middle part of the body. In dancing, especially in the Oriental style of dancing, which is the mimic representation of animated feeling, the breast and the body are raised, and the forms of the body appear through the clothing.
entries.269140612b21700e32bbd5593c971e8cb221cb73: Sol 7:2 2 Thy navel is a well-rounded basin -    Let not mixed wine be wanting to it    Thy body is a heap of wheat,    Set round with lilies. <div eID="gen12669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12670" type="x-p"/> In interpreting these words, Hitzig proceeds as if a “voluptuary” were here speaking. He therefore changes שׁררך into שׁררך, “thy <hi type="italic">pudenda</hi>.” But (1) it is no voluptuary who speaks here, and particularly not a man, but women who speak; certainly, above all, it is the poet, who would not, however, be so inconsiderate as to put into the mouths of women immodest words which he could use if he wished to represent the king as speaking. Moreover (2) שׁר = (Arab.) surr, secret (that which is secret; in Arab. especially referred to the pudenda, both of man and woman), is a word that is<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Tebrîzi, in my work entitled <hi type="italic">Jud.-Arab. Poesien, u.s.w</hi>. (1874), p. 24.</note> foreign to the Heb. language, which has for “Geheimnis” secret the corresponding word סוד (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Ps.2.2">Psa 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.25.14">Psa 25:14</reference>), after the root-signification of its verbal stem (viz., to be firm, pressed together); and (3) the reference - preferred by Döpke, Magnus, Hahn, and others, also without any change of punctuation - of שׁר to the <hi type="italic">interfeminium mulieris</hi>, is here excluded by the circumstance that the attractions of a woman dancing, as they unfold themselves, are here described. Like the Arab. surr, שׁר (= shurr), from שׁרר, to bind fast, denotes properly the umbilical cord, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.4">Eze 16:4</reference>, and then the umbilical scar. Thus, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.8">Pro 3:8</reference>, where most recent critics prefer, for לשׁרּך, to read, but without any proper reason, לשׁרך = לשׁארך, “to thy flesh,” the navel comes there into view as the centre of the body, - which it always is with new-born infants, and is almost so with grown-up persons in respect of the length of the body, - and as, indeed, the centre. whence the pleasurable feeling of health diffuses its rays of heat. This middle and prominent point of the abdomen shows itself in one lightly clad and dancing when she breathes deeply, even through the clothing; and because the navel commonly forms a little funnel-like hollow (Böttch.: in the form almost of a whirling hollow in the water, as one may see in nude antique statues), therefore the daughters of Jerusalem compare Shulamith’s navel to a “basin of roundness,” <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, which has this general property, and thus belongs to the class of things that are round. אגּן does not mean a <hi type="italic">Becher</hi> (a cup), but a <hi type="italic">Bechen</hi> (basin), <hi type="italic">pelvis</hi>; properly a washing basin, ijjanah (from אגן = ajan, to full, to wash = כּבּס); then a sprinkling basin, <reference osisRef="Exod.24.6">Exo 24:6</reference>; and generally a basin, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.24">Isa 22:24</reference>; here, a mixing basin, in which wine was mingled with a proportion of water to render it palatable (κρατήρ, from κεραννύναι, <hi type="italic">temperare</hi>), - according to the Talm. with two-thirds of water. In this sense this passage is interpreted allegorically, <hi type="italic">Sanhedrin</hi> 14 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, 37 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, and elsewhere (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Aruch under מזג). מזג .)מז is not spiced wine, which is otherwise designated (Sol 8:2), but, as Hitzig rightly explains, mixed wine, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, mixed with water or snow (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Isa.5.22">Isa 5:22</reference>). מזג is not borrowed from the Greek μίσγειν (Grätz), but is a word native to all the three chief Semitic dialects, - the weaker form of מסך, which may have the meaning of “to pour in;” but not merely “to pour in,” but, at that same time, “to mix” (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Isa.5.22">Isa 5:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.9.2">Pro 9:2</reference>). סהר, with אגּן, represents the circular form (from סהר = סחר), corresponding to the navel ring; Kimchi thinks that the moon must be understood (cf. שׂהרון, lunula): a moon-like round basin; according to which the Venet., also in Gr., choosing an excellent name for the moon, translates: ῥἀντιστρον τῆς ἑκάτης. But “moon-basin” would be an insufficient expression for it; Ewald supposes that it is the name of a flower, without, however, establishing this opinion. The “basin of roundness” is the centre of the body a little depressed; and that which the clause, “may not mixed wine be lacking,” expresses, as their wish for her, is soundness of health, for which no more appropriate and delicate figure can be given than hot wine tempered with fresh water. <div eID="gen12670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12671" type="x-p"/> The comparison in 3b is the same as that of R. Johanan’s of beauty, <hi type="italic">Mezîa</hi> 84 <hi type="italic">a</hi>: “He who would gain an idea of beauty should take a silver cup, fill it with pomegranate flowers, and encircle its rim with a garland of roses.”<note placement="foot">See my <hi type="italic">Gesch. d. Jüd. Poesie</hi>, p. 30 f. Hoch (the German Solomon) reminds us of the Jewish marriage custom of throwing over the newly-married pair the contents of a vessel wreathed with flowers, and filled with wheat or corn (with money underneath), accompanied with the cry, פּרוּ וּרבוּ be fruitful and multiply.</note> <div eID="gen12671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12672" type="x-p"/> To the present day, winnowed and sifted corn is piled up in great heaps of symmetrical half-spherical form, which are then frequently stuck over with things that move in the wind, for the purpose of protecting them against birds. “The appearance of such heaps of wheat,” says Wetstein (<hi type="italic">Isa</hi>. p. 710), “which one may see in long parallel rows on the thrashing-floors of a village, is very pleasing to a peasant; and the comparison of the Song; Sol 7:3, every Arabian will regard as beautiful.” Such a corn-heap is to the present day called ṣubbah, while ‛aramah is a heap of thrashed corn that has not yet been winnowed; here, with ערמה, is to be connected the idea of a ṣubbah, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, of a heap of wheat not only thrashed and winnowed, but also sifted (riddled). סוּג, enclosed, fenced about (whence the post-bibl. סיג, a fence), is a part. pass. such as פּוּץ, scattered (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Ps.92.12">Psa 92:12</reference>). The comparison refers to the beautiful appearance of the roundness, but, at the same time, also the flesh-colour shining through the dress; for fancy sees more than the eyes, and concludes regarding that which is veiled from that which is visible. A wheat-colour was, according to the Moslem Sunna, the tint of the first created man. Wheat-yellow and lily-white is a subdued white, and denotes at once purity and health; by πυρός wheat one thinks of πῦρ - heaped up wheat developes a remarkable heat, a fact for which Biesenthal refers to Plutarch’s <hi type="italic">Quaest</hi>. In accordance with the progress of the description, the breasts are now spoken of:
entries.3eb5add95b93e216f1d744012b5181ad4112cf2c: Sol 7:3 3 Thy two breasts are like two fawns,    Twins of a gazelle. <div eID="gen12672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12673" type="x-p"/> Sol 4:5 is repeated, but with the omission of the attribute, “feeding among lilies,” since lilies have already been applied to another figure. Instead of תּאומי there, we have here מּאמי (taǒme), the former after the ground-form ti'âm, the latter after the ground-form to'm (cf. נּאלי, <reference osisRef="Neh.8.2">Neh 8:2</reference>, from גּאל = גּאל).
entries.15864ac6f02a8061dc16b8194b39c33964293420: Sol 7:4 4a Thy neck like an ivory tower. <div eID="gen12673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12674" type="x-p"/> The article in חשּׁן may be that designating species (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under Sol 1:11); but, as at Sol 7:5 and Sol 4:4, it appears to be also here a definite tower which the comparison has in view: one covered externally with ivory tablets, a tower well known to all in and around Jerusalem, and visible far and wide, especially when the sun shone on it; had it been otherwise, as in the case of the comparison following, the locality would have been more definitely mentioned. So slender, so dazzlingly white, is imposing, and so captivating to the eye did Shulamith’s neck appear. These and the following figures would be open to the objection of being without any occasion, and monstrous, if they referred to an ordinary beauty; but they refer to Solomon’s spouse, they apply to a queen, and therefore are derived from that which is most splendid in the kingdom over which, along with him, she rules; and in this they have the justification of their grandeur. 4 <hi type="italic">b</hi>a Thine eyes pools in Heshbon,        At the gate of the populous (city).<hi type="italic">Hesbhon</hi>, formerly belonging to the Amorites, but at this time to the kingdom of Solomon, lay about 5 1/2 hours to the east of the northern point of the Dead Sea, on an extensive, undulating, fruitful, high table-land, with a far-reaching prospect. Below the town, now existing only in heaps of ruins, a brook, which here takes it rise, flows westward, and streams toward the Ghôr as the <hi type="italic">Nahr Hesbán</hi>. It joins the Jordan not far above its entrance into the Dead Sea. The situation of the town was richly watered. There still exists a huge reservoir of excellent masonry in the valley, about half a mile from the foot of the hill on which the town stood. The comparison here supposes two such pools, but which are not necessarily together, though both are before the gate, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, near by, outside the town. Since שׁער, except at <reference osisRef="Isa.14.31">Isa 14:31</reference>, is fem., רבּים־בּים, in the sense of עם רבּתי, <reference osisRef="Lam.1.1">Lam 1:1</reference> (cf. for the non-determin. of the adj., <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.25">Eze 21:25</reference>), is to be referred to the town, not to the gate (Hitz.); Blau's<note placement="foot">In Merx' <hi type="italic">Archiv.</hi> III 355.</note> conjectural reading, bath-'akrabbim, does not recommend itself, because the craggy heights of the “ascent of Akrabbim” (Num 34:4; <reference osisRef="Josh.15.3">Jos 15:3</reference>), which obliquely cross<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Robinson’s <hi type="italic">Phys. Geogr.</hi> p. 51.</note> the Ghôr to the south of the Dead Sea, and from remote times formed the southern boundary of the kingdom of the Amorites (Jdg 1:36), were too far off, and too seldom visited, to give its name to a gate of Heshbon. But generally the crowds of men at the gate and the topography of the gate are here nothing to the purpose; the splendour of the town, however, is for the figure of the famed cisterns like a golden border. בּרכה (from בּרך, to spread out, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Genesis</hi>, p. 98; Fleischer in <hi type="italic">Levy</hi>, I 420 <hi type="italic">b</hi>) denotes a skilfully built round or square pool. The comparison of the eyes to a pool means, as Wetstein<note placement="foot">Zeitschr. <hi type="italic">für allgem. Erdkunde</hi>, 1859, p. 157 f.</note> remarks, “either thus glistening like a water-mirror, or thus lovely in appearance, for the Arabian knows no greater pleasure than to look upon clear, gently rippling water.” Both are perhaps to be taken together; the mirroring glance of the moist eyes (cf. Ovid, <hi type="italic">De Arte Am</hi>. ii. 722):<hi type="italic">“Adspicies obulos tremulo fulgore micantes, Ut sol a liquida saepe refulget aqua”</hi> and the spell of the charm holding fast the gaze of the beholder. 4 <hi type="italic">b</hi>b Thy nose like the tower of Lebanon,        Which looks towards Damascus. <div eID="gen12674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12675" type="x-p"/> This comparison also places us in the midst of the architectural and artistic splendours of the Solomonic reign. A definite town is here meant; the art. determines it, and the part. following appositionally without the art., with the expression “towards Damascus” defining it more nearly (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under Sol 3:6), describes it. הלּמנון designates here “the whole Alpine range of mountains in the north of the land of Israel” (Furrer); for a tower which looks in the direction of Damascus (פּני, accus., as את־פּני,   <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.4">1Sa 22:4</reference>) is to be thought of as standing on one of the eastern spurs of Hermon, or on the top of Amana (Sol 4:8), whence the Amana (Barada) takes its rise, whether as a watch-tower (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.6">2Sa 8:6</reference>), or only as a look-out from which might be enjoyed the paradisaical prospect. The nose gives to the face especially its physiognomical expression, and conditions its beauty. Its comparison to a tower on a lofty height is occasioned by the fact that Shulamith’s nose, without being blunt or flat, formed a straight line from the brow downward, without bending to the right or left (Hitzig), a mark of symmetrical beauty combined with awe-inspiring dignity. After the praise of the nose it was natural to think of Carmel; Carmel is a promontory, and as such is called anf el-jebel (“nose of the mountain-range”).
entries.ffe2d2cd2978524d11e513ce770fcb388e442eae: Sol 7:5 5 <hi type="italic">a</hi>a Thy head upon thee as Carmel. <div eID="gen12675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12676" type="x-p"/> We say that the head is “on the man” (2Ki 6:31; Judith 14:18), for we think of a man ideally as the central unity of the members forming the external appearance of his body. Shulamith’s head ruled her form, surpassing all in beauty and majesty, as Carmel with its noble and pleasing appearance ruled the land and sea at its feet. From the summit of Carmel, clothed with trees) <reference osisRef="Amos.9.3">Amo 9:3</reference>; 1Ki 18:42), a transition is made to the hair on the head, which the Moslem poets are fond of comparing to long leaves, as vine leaves and palm branches; as, on the other hand, the thick leafy wood is called (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Isa.7.20">Isa 7:20</reference>) <hi type="italic">comata silva</hi> (cf. Oudendorp’s Apuleii <hi type="italic">Metam</hi>. p. 744). Grätz, proceeding on the supposition of the existence of Persian words in the Song, regards כרמל as the name of a colour; but (1) crimson is designated in the Heb.-Pers. not כרמל, but כרמיל, instead of תולעת שׁני (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Isa.1.18">Isa 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.31.21">Pro 31:21</reference>); (<reference osisRef="Prov.31.2">2</reference>) if the hair of the head (if ראשׁך might be directly understood of this) may indeed be compared to the glistening of purple, not, however, to the listening of carmese or scarlet, then red and not black hair must be meant. But it is not the locks of hair, but the hair in locks that is meant. From this the eulogium finally passes to the hair of the head itself. 5 <hi type="italic">a</hi>b The flowing hair of thy head like purple -        A king fettered by locks. <div eID="gen12676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12677" type="x-p"/> Hitzig supposes that כרמל reminded the poet of כּרמיל (carmese), and that thus he hit upon ארגּמן (purple); but one would rather think that <hi type="italic">Carmel</hi> itself would immediately lead him to purple, for near this promontory is the principal place where purple shell-fish are found (Seetzen’s <hi type="italic">Reisen</hi>, IV 277 f.). דּלּה (from דּלל, to dangle, to hang loose, <reference osisRef="Job.28.4">Job 28:4</reference>, Arab. tadladal) is <hi type="italic">res pendula</hi>, and particularly <hi type="italic">coma pendula</hi>. Hengst. remarks that the “purple” has caused much trouble to those who understand by דלה the hair of the head. He himself, with Gussetius, understand by it the temples,<hi type="italic">tempus capitis</hi>; but the word רקּה is used (Sol 4:3) for “temples,” and “purple-like” hair hanging down could occasion trouble only to those who know not how to distinguish purple from carmese. Red purple, ארגּמן (Assyr. argamannu, Aram., Arab., Pers., with departure from the primary meaning of the word, ארגּון ,drow eht), which derives this name from רגם = רקם, material of variegated colour, is dark-red, and almost glistening black, as Pliny says (<hi type="italic">Hist. Nat</hi>. ix. 135): <hi type="italic">Laus ei</hi> (the Tyrian purple) <hi type="italic">summa in colore sanguinis concreti, nigricans adspectu idemque suspectu (seen from the side) refulgens, unde et Homero purpureus dicitur sanguis</hi>. The purple hair of Nisus does not play a part in myth alone, but beautiful shining dark black hair is elsewhere also called purple, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, πυρφύρεος πλόκαμος in Lucian, πορφυραῖ χαῖται in Anacreon.
